title: Mortal and venial sin (CCC 1854–1861)
hookLine: grave matter, full knowledge, full consent; lesser sins wound but don't kill love

cards: A friendship, and two ways it can go wrong. You forget their birthday. You're short with them on a bad day.
You cancel plans twice. None of it is good, and all of it strains things. But the friendship survives: it's wounded, and a little apology heals it.
Then something else: you betray them, knowingly, on purpose, in something that really matters. That doesn't strain the friendship. It breaks it.
The Catholic Church uses exactly that difference to talk about sin. The phrase mortal sin can sound frightening. Today, what it actually means.

teach.h: A SIN UNTO DEATH, AND ONE NOT.
teach.b: The First Letter of John speaks of a sin that leads to death, and sins that don't. The Church has long read this as a real difference between sins, and the Catechism names them: mortal and venial. Mortal means deadly.
The Catechism says mortal sin destroys charity, the love of God, in the heart.
And three conditions must all be met at once. Grave matter: something serious, the kind of thing the Ten Commandments name. Full knowledge: knowing it's seriously wrong.
Deliberate consent: choosing it freely, on purpose. All three, not one or two.

Venial comes from the Latin venia, pardon: forgivable. It's the forgotten birthday, the sharp word, the small dishonesty. The Catechism says venial sin wounds and weakens charity but doesn't destroy it.
It still matters, because small habits can grow, but it doesn't break the friendship. Then what softens the picture, and what heals it.
Ignorance you couldn't help, strong emotions, outside pressure and illness can lessen how responsible a person is, the Catechism says.
And it adds a line that's easy to miss: we can judge that an act is gravely wrong, but the judgment of persons belongs to God alone.
As for healing, Catholics believe even mortal sin can be forgiven, above all in confession. The distinction isn't there to make people afraid.
It's there so they can tell a wound from a break, and not treat every scrape as the end of the world, or a real break as nothing.

how: Catholics confess mortal sins in the sacrament of reconciliation, and are encouraged to confess venial sins too; at the start of Mass, the penitential act asks forgiveness for everyday sins.

o: any sin committed by a mortal human being
a grave sin, knowingly chosen, that breaks with God
a sin that brings sudden death as punishment

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: any sin can be mortal if it's serious enough, even without knowing it
all three are needed: grave matter, full knowledge, deliberate consent.
the Catechism says only God judges persons
we can judge an act is gravely wrong, but the judgment of persons belongs to God.
Catholics believe mortal sin can't be forgiven
Catholics believe it can be forgiven, above all in confession.

games.q: someone does something seriously wrong, but truly didn't know it was wrong and couldn't have known. by the Catechism's three conditions, is it a mortal sin?
games.why: all three conditions must be met. ignorance a person couldn't help can lessen or even remove responsibility.

practice: Think back over the last week and name one small thing you regret, a word, an impatience, a shortcut: wounded, not broken.

Then gently ask whether there's anything heavier, something that feels like a break; if there is, don't panic, just notice it, and know that Catholics believe there's a door back. If you pray, you can ask for mercy for both.

wordCard.voice: Mortal sin. A sin that breaks the friendship with God: grave matter, chosen with full knowledge and deliberate consent. Catholics believe it can be forgiven.

orig.note: Greek, 1 John 5:16: sin unto death, the root of the Church's mortal and venial distinction.

carryVoice: Your line: wounds and breaks. And for both, Catholics say, a door back. See you tomorrow.
